Mississippi Property Tax Guide: Appeals, Exemptions and Selling With Tax Due

Selling a Mississippi House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Mississippi?
We buy Mississippi houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

How the tax is figured

Three numbers multiply to make your bill: the property's true value, an assessment ratio fixed by the state constitution, and the millage rate where the property sits. Everything gets sorted into one of five classes, and the class picks the ratio.

  • Class I: the single-family house an owner occupies, at 10%.
  • Class II: any other real estate outside Class I and IV, at 15%.
  • Class III is personal property, except vehicles and anything in Class IV. Ratio: 15%.
  • Class IV is public utility property. Ratio: 30%.
  • Class V is cars and trucks. Ratio: 30%.

One mill equals a thousandth of a dollar. The house you live in sits in Class I. Vacant land or a rental falls into Class II and gets the heavier 15% ratio. If you inherited a parent's house and nobody lives in it now, ask the Tax Assessor which class it will land in.

Who does what

Your bill passes through four county offices. The Tax Assessor puts a number on the property. The Tax Collector receives your check. The Chancery Clerk keeps the deed records and conducts the delinquent sale. The Board of Supervisors listens to complaints and signs off on the final rolls. The state mostly watches.

  • Counties, cities and some school boards each choose their own millage.
  • Expect a county line and a school district line on every bill, with another for a city or levee district if the parcel is inside one.
  • Voters in each of five districts elect one county supervisor.
  • Oversight splits: the Department of Revenue audits the appraisal work, while the State Auditor watches collection.

Because rates stack by location, a house in town and an equally valued house outside it will not be billed the same.

Due dates and penalties

The assessment goes to the person on title as of January 1. Bills are mailed in November or December and must be paid by February 1 of the following year. Should that date be a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, paying on the next Monday costs nothing extra.

Property tax calendar
EventWhen it happens
Owner of record is fixed for assessmentJanuary 1
Window to file for homestead exemptionJanuary 1 through April 1
Deed or other ownership paper recorded for the exemptionFiled before January 7
Last day to appeal value to the Board of SupervisorsUsually the first Monday in August
Tax statements mailedNovember or December
Payment deadlineFebruary 1 the next year
Delinquent property auctionFirst Monday in April or last Monday in August, set by county

Land and buildings are reappraised at least once in four years. Taxable personal property is reappraised annually. An assessor is not required to enter your house, though a walk around the grounds is allowed and a barn that has seen better days still counts.

Homestead exemption

Living in the house as your primary residence? Visit the county Tax Assessor between January 1 and April 1 to claim homestead exemption. Once approved, you do not file again until something about your situation changes.

  • Tier 1 is a credit, never more than $300, for applicants under 65 who fall outside the disability tier.
  • Tier 2 is built for owners who have reached 65 or are totally disabled by January 1. No tax is charged on the first $7,500 of assessed value, a figure the state also states as $75,000 of true value.
  • Tier 3 means no property tax at all. It is open to service-connected totally disabled former service members, honorably discharged ones who have reached 90, and certain unremarried spouses of service members killed on active duty.

You have to own the home and live there on January 1, with title already recorded before that. A new deed, a divorce, a death, or a different use of the home may mean filing again. Behind on state income tax returns, or vehicles tagged somewhere else? Either can cost you the exemption, and the amount wrongly excused may be billed back to you.

If you close after January 1 and the bill is still open, the tax was assessed to you as the earlier owner. Ask the closing agent to split it on the settlement statement.

How to appeal your assessment

If the value on your notice looks wrong, you can request a hearing before the county Board of Supervisors. Your Chancery Clerk explains the local procedure. Most counties expect the request by the first Monday in August.

Supervisors review the assessor's values, listen to taxpayer objections and adopt the rolls. Keep these points in mind while you prepare:

  • The hearing covers worth only. Rates are decided elsewhere, by the county, city and school district.
  • An assessor who measured the house wrong may owe you a refund on earlier years. The Chancery Clerk can tell you.
  • A jump on your bill can come from the value, the rate, or the two together.

If a sale is coming, find out from the Chancery Clerk and Tax Collector what happens to an open appeal, and have the title company verify the amount you owe.

When the tax is not paid

Late payments pick up penalties and interest. A parcel that stays delinquent is offered at the county tax auction, which happens on one of two dates, first Monday in April or last Monday in August, based on the county.

The Chancery Clerk runs each year's sale, keeps the paperwork, and can quote the cost of redeeming a parcel that was sold. A parcel with no buyer goes to the State of Mississippi, with the Secretary of State as manager. Their phone number is 1-866-835-2637.

The county tax collector fields sale questions. Owing back tax? Request the balance and any redemption amount early, so closing day holds no surprises.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Mississippi houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Paying the bill and what to bring

Start by assembling documents. The tax bill itself shows the parcel and the millage that applies. The legal description comes from the Chancery Clerk. Receipts for earlier years help if a title company asks for proof that nothing is open.

Then work through the offices in order. The Tax Assessor answers value and class questions. The Tax Collector knows the balance and how to pay it. The Chancery Clerk is the contact for appeals, land records and the tax sale. Keep a short note of who you spoke with and when, since closing agents often ask for it, and if you decide to sell to a cash buyer the same notes make the process faster.

Selling with taxes owed

Three snags come up again and again: last year's bill is still unpaid, the homestead exemption lapsed or was never claimed, or an empty house has changed class. For an inherited house that no one occupies, the question for the Tax Assessor is whether the ratio now jumps from 10% to 15% of true value.

  • Request the bill from the Tax Collector and the legal description from the Chancery Clerk.
  • Find out whether homestead was ever claimed, and whether a disallowance is waiting.
  • Ask the title company to review this year's bill along with any tax sale past.
  • For a house still in probate, read our Mississippi probate guide on who may sign.

A realistic sequence helps. First learn what is owed and whether the class or exemption is correct. Second, settle or schedule the payment so no lien surprises the buyer. Third, hand the title company the receipts. Skipping the first step is where most delays begin, because a buyer who finds an old balance at the last minute may ask for time or a lower price.

Our company buys houses across Mississippi in their current condition, even with tax owing or repairs put off, and answers with a written offer. Nothing here promises a price.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Mississippi property tax rate?

Mississippi has no one statewide rate. A parcel pays county and school district millage, and sometimes a city or special district rate on top. Multiply true value by the assessment ratio and then by total millage; owner-occupied homes carry a 10% ratio.

When are Mississippi property taxes due?

February 1 is the deadline for the property assessed the year before. When it falls on a weekend or legal holiday, paying the next Monday avoids penalty and interest.

Can I appeal my Mississippi property assessment?

Yes. Go through the Chancery Clerk to get a hearing in front of the county Board of Supervisors. The usual filing date is the first Monday in August, which comes before the bill is due.

When must I apply for homestead exemption in Mississippi?

Apply with the county Tax Assessor, anytime from January 1 to April 1. A filing that arrives later is too late for that year.

Can I sell a house in Mississippi with property tax due?

You can. Cash buyers often take a house in its current shape, and the title company will confirm what is owed when you close. Left alone, unpaid tax can lead to a county auction, so find out the balance first.

content:
Mississippi Homestead Exemption: Eligibility, Filing and Selling the Home

Cash Home Buyers in Mississippi
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Mississippi Homestead Exemption: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Mississippi Homestead Exemption sale
  • Turn the Mississippi Homestead Exemption offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Mississippi House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Mississippi?
We buy Mississippi houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Homestead exemption basics

Mississippi's homestead exemption trims the annual property tax on the home where you live. Nothing happens automatically: the owner files, and the size of the break turns on which of three tiers fits. The governing statutes run from Mississippi Code Section 27-33-1 through Section 27-33-79.

Only the tax bill moves. Market value and the price a buyer pays stay where they were. The exemption still deserves attention before a sale, because an exemption that gets disallowed can be charged back to the owner for earlier years, and a lender reviewing the buyer's file may look at that history.

Who qualifies and when to apply

Filing happens at the county Tax Assessor's office, between January 1 and April 1. On January 1 you must already hold title and occupy the house as your primary residence. The assessor accepts applications at the counter during regular business hours only. Miss April 1 and that assessment year is gone.

  • Title must be in place before January 1, with the ownership instrument filed at the Chancery Clerk before January 7.
  • You need to fit the head of family definition in Section 27-33-13 and own the home in a form Section 27-33-17 accepts.
  • Both spouses must be current with state income tax law and the road and bridge privilege tax law.
  • Service members posted outside Mississippi can qualify when they claim the state as home and comply with its laws. A married servicemember needs both spouses to qualify.

What to bring to the assessor

Gather a Social Security number or ITIN for each applicant, birth dates, phone and mailing details, the street address of the property (a P.O. box will not do), the purchase price and down payment, the HUD closing statement or a similar document, and the tag number of every vehicle you own.

Tier 2 filers also need proof of age, like a driver's license or birth certificate, or proof of total disability. Disability can be shown by a classification under the Social Security Act, the Railroad Retirement Act, or a qualified retirement plan, by IRS Schedule 3 and Schedule R, or by a detailed letter from two physicians.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Mississippi house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What each tier saves

Mississippi homestead exemption tiers
TierWho it coversBenefit
Tier 1, regularQualified applicants under 65 who do not qualify for a disability tierTax credit of up to $300, based on property value
Tier 2, age or disabilityAt least 65 or totally disabled by January 1 of the filing yearExempt from tax on the first $7,500 of assessed value
Tier 3, totalService-connected totally disabled, honorably discharged former service members, anyone 90 or older, and certain unremarried surviving spousesExempt from all property taxes on the qualifying homestead

Tier 2 is sometimes described as covering the first $75,000 of true value. Because a single-family owner-occupied house is assessed at 10 percent, that works out to the same $7,500 of assessed value. After year one, the Tier 2 exemption can stretch to absorb most later increases in value.

Reapplying and renewals

Once your application is approved, the credit continues year after year with no refiling, unless you lose it or a change has occurred since January 1 of the preceding year. Any of the following sends you back to the assessor with a new application:

  • A different property description, owner, use, or occupant.
  • Marriage, divorce, remarriage, death, or a new deed.
  • A shift in disability or VA benefit eligibility.
  • Moving up a tier, for example by turning 65, which you handle in the next filing period.

If you are unsure whether a change counts, call the Tax Assessor before April 1. Once the window closes, no refund is available to repair a late filing for that year.

How the exemption gets taken away

Any slip in the underlying requirements can lead to disallowance, and the bill can land on you. The usual causes:

  • Skipping or paying late on Mississippi income tax, or filing as a non-resident.
  • Registering vehicles somewhere else. Cars and trucks are supposed to be tagged where they are domiciled, which is the homestead address.
  • Taking homestead on a second property.
  • Staying silent after a change in the description, owner, use, or occupancy.

When an exemption is disallowed, you may owe the taxing jurisdictions what was wrongly excused. Later assessments, mortgage payments, and escrow payments can all be affected, and collection efforts can follow. Settle any dispute before the listing goes up.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Mississippi houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling a home that has the exemption

The exemption belongs to the owner, not the property. When title changes hands, the new owner needs a new application, filed in the next January 1 to April 1 window if they plan to live there.

The tax calendar runs like this: assessment to the owner of record on January 1, bills out in November and December, payment due February 1. For a closing in the middle of the year, ask the closing agent how that year's tax gets divided between you and the buyer.

If you moved out and turned the place into a rental, plan on losing the exemption, since the applicant has to be living there on January 1. Real property that is not single-family owner-occupied is assessed at 15 percent rather than 10 percent. For a cash sale, current taxes matter too. An as-is buyer will want proof of payment, because a delinquent balance can end in the county tax sale and a two-year redemption period under Section 27-45-3.

Why the dates matter to a seller

Three calendar points drive most of the confusion. January 1 fixes who owns the house and where they live. January 7 is the cutoff for getting the ownership paper to the Chancery Clerk. April 1 closes the filing window. A family deed or a purchase that lands near those dates can shift which year the exemption starts, so a seller who is also transferring title to a relative should talk to the Tax Assessor before signing anything.

Buyers who plan to occupy the home usually only need to learn one thing from you: file promptly once they own it. Passing along the assessor's contact details and the filing window costs nothing and helps them avoid a lost year.

A short checklist before you list

  1. Phone the Tax Assessor and confirm the exemption is active and which tier you hold.
  2. Ask whether any disallowance or repayment demand is on file for the house.
  3. Get the current bill from the Tax Collector and pay it if it is open.
  4. Let the closing agent know the buyer must file their own application next window.

A few phone calls now beat a scramble at the title company, and that holds for a traditional listing as much as for a cash offer.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

When is the Mississippi homestead exemption deadline?

April 1. The county Tax Assessor takes applications from January 1 through April 1 only, and you must have owned and lived in the home on January 1.

How much is the homestead exemption in Mississippi?

It varies by tier. Tier 1 is a credit of up to $300, Tier 2 exempts the first $7,500 of assessed value for owners 65 or older or totally disabled, and Tier 3 exempts all property tax for qualifying disabled former service members and certain surviving spouses.

Do I need to reapply for the homestead exemption every year?

No. An approved exemption carries forward until ownership, use, occupancy, or the property description changes, or you move into a different tier.

Can I keep the exemption if I rent out my house?

Probably not. The applicant has to own and occupy the home as a primary residence on January 1. Call the county Tax Assessor before claiming it on a rented house, because an improper claim can be disallowed.

Does the buyer get my homestead exemption?

No. Ownership changes require a new application, and the buyer files with the county Tax Assessor in the next January 1 to April 1 window.

title: Mississippi Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling
content:
Mississippi Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

Cash Home Buyers in Mississippi
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Mississippi Estate and Inheritance Tax sale
  • Turn the Mississippi Estate and Inheritance Tax offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Mississippi House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Mississippi?
We buy Mississippi houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

No state estate or inheritance tax

Mississippi does not tax inheritances or gifts, and an estate of someone who died on or after January 1, 2005 owes no state estate return. Home values here run modest: $169,800 is the median for an owner-occupied house.

The state once collected an estate tax that piggybacked on a federal credit for state death taxes. Starting with 2005 deaths, Congress turned that credit into a deduction, and the Mississippi levy faded out with it. Leftover estate tax provisions remain in Title 27, Chapter 9, and apportionment rules live in Title 27, Chapter 10.

An heir listing the house therefore will not get a state tax bill for receiving it. Money questions come from elsewhere: federal rules aimed at very large estates, income tax on a profit at sale, the yearly land tax, and recording costs.

Federal estate tax and a typical home

Washington taxes only the biggest estates. The 2026 filing threshold is $15,000,000, and the Form 706 instructions pair that exclusion with a basic credit amount of $5,945,800.

Gifts have their own yearly cap of $19,000 for each recipient across 2025 and 2026. Both figures concern the person who died. If a federal return is due at all, the executor files it, not the heir.

An ordinary Mississippi house sits far under that line. The house matters only when every account and asset in the estate, added together, climbs past the threshold.

Tax amounts at a glance

Mississippi and federal limits
Tax or amountRule
State estate returnNone for deaths on or after January 1, 2005
State inheritance and gift taxesNone
Federal estate filing threshold (2026 deaths)$15,000,000
Federal basic credit amount (2026)$5,945,800
Gift exclusion per donee (2025 to 2026)$19,000
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Mississippi house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Capital gain when an heir sells

Income tax lands on the profit alone, so the question is what the heir's cost basis is. For inherited real estate, basis usually equals the home's fair market value at the date of death, with or without an estate tax return.

A sale above that figure produces a taxable gain, reported on Schedule D and Form 8949. Where the executor files Form 706, heirs may receive a Schedule A to Form 8971, and the basis can then be tied to the value used for the estate tax.

That is the reason an appraisal as of the death date helps even in an estate that owes nothing. It anchors the gain calculation. Your executor or a tax preparer can tell you which value governs.

  • File the death-date appraisal or valuation letter with your closing papers.
  • Save the settlement statement, because selling costs shrink the gain.
  • Find out from the executor whether a Schedule A to Form 8971 went out.

Property tax on the inherited house

The land tax attaches to the parcel, whoever happens to own it. Each assessment goes to the owner of record as of January 1, bills go out in November or December, and payment is due the following February 1.

When a parent dies in autumn and the house is still titled in the estate, that year's bill still comes due on schedule. The Tax Collector computes it as true value, times the assessment ratio, times the millage rate. An owner-occupied single-family home is Class I and is assessed at 10 percent of true value. Once nobody lives there, it drops out of that category into the 15 percent class for other real property.

Skipped payments can end in a sale at the county tax auction, with two years after the sale for the owner to redeem under Section 27-45-3. If the house sat for years without payment, check its status before you advertise it.

Does the homestead exemption survive the owner's death?

No, not by itself. An exemption carries forward year after year until something changes, and a death, a new deed or a change in who occupies the home can all call for a fresh application.

Applications run from January 1 through April 1 at the county Tax Assessor, and the applicant must own the home and live in it as a primary residence on January 1. Tiers are covered in our Mississippi homestead exemption guide. A buyer must file a new application after you sell.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Mississippi houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Chancery clerk: estate file and land records

One office, the county chancery clerk, keeps both the probate-style estate file and the deed books. The Chancery Court there hears estates, guardianships, conservatorships, divorces and similar equity cases, and the Recording Department files deeds, deeds of trust, releases, liens and lis pendens.

Because the clerk guards the public land records, assessors rely on them to identify each parcel's owner. Record any deed to heirs or to a buyer promptly, so the tax rolls name the true owner.

The legislature fixes the recording charge. A sample clerk schedule effective January 1, 2020 under Section 25-7-9 prices a deed at $26.00 in a county that collects an archive fee and $25.00 in one that does not, covering five pages, with $1.00 for every page after. Phone the clerk in your county for today's price.

From estate file to closing

A sale usually moves in a fixed sequence. First the estate file at chancery court shows who holds authority. Next the deed into the heirs, if one is needed, goes to the clerk for recording so the land records match the family. Then the Tax Collector confirms nothing is owed on the parcel, and the closing agent splits the current year's land tax between the two sides.

A cash purchase shortens the buyer's side of this, since there is no lender appraisal or loan underwriting to wait on, and the house can go as-is. The estate side stays the same. Signing authority, a clean tax record and a recorded deed are still needed before funds change hands, and no state estate tax filing has to be cleared first.

Checklist before listing an inherited house

Work in this order: title, then taxes, then the buyer. No state estate tax stands in the way, so delays usually come from paperwork and liens.

  • Establish who is allowed to sign, which normally traces back to the chancery court estate file.
  • Request the county tax record and ask the Tax Collector about any unpaid balance.
  • See whether the parcel ever went to a tax sale and whether the two-year redemption period is still running.
  • Obtain a value as of the death date for your basis.
  • Ask the clerk what recording a deed costs.
  • Ask the closing agent how this year's property tax will be split between you and the buyer.

Cash buyers will take an inherited house as-is, handy when repairs are more than the family wants to pay for. All the steps above still apply, and nobody should quote you a price until the title and any liens are clear.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Is there an inheritance tax in Mississippi?

No. Mississippi levies no inheritance or gift tax, and deaths on or after January 1, 2005 require no state estate return.

When does the federal estate tax apply to a Mississippi estate?

Only to very large estates, starting at $15,000,000 for a 2026 death. A normal house is well below that, but the threshold counts everything the person owned.

Do I pay tax when I sell a house I inherited in Mississippi?

Possibly federal income tax on the profit. The basis is normally the home's value at the date of death, so only the sale price above that amount is gain.

Who pays the property tax on a house in an estate?

Whoever owns the house when the bill is due. Ownership is fixed as of January 1, with payment due by February 1 of the next year, so confirm the balance with the county Tax Collector.

Does the homestead exemption transfer to my heirs?

Not automatically. A death or deed change can require a new application, filed between January 1 and April 1.

How a residential eviction works in Mississippi

A landlord must give written notice, file a sworn affidavit or complaint in court, win a judgment, and then have the sheriff or a constable carry out a warrant of removal. The rules for homes and apartments sit in the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, Title 89, Chapter 8 of the Mississippi Code.

That chapter was rewritten in 2022 and amended again in 2025, so check any older summary against the current text. Section 89-8-31 allows a landlord to start eviction proceedings for breach of the rental agreement or for failing to vacate after the agreement ends. Nothing in the chapter lets an owner skip the court step.

The older Chapter 7 sections, including 89-7-27, apply to premises that are not a dwelling unit, such as commercial space. If you own a rented house, Chapter 8 is the one that governs.

Notice a landlord must give

The notice period depends on why the tenancy is ending. Notice must be in writing, and email or text counts only if the tenant agreed in writing to be notified that way.

Mississippi notice periods by situation
SituationNotice required
Unpaid rentWritten notice that the agreement ends if rent is not paid within 3 days
Other material breach by tenantTermination date not less than 14 days after receipt, if not fixed within a reasonable time up to 14 days
Month-to-month tenancy30 days written notice
Week-to-week tenancy7 days written notice
Substantial violation affecting health or safetyNo notice required

A breach that can be repaired is treated differently. Under Section 89-8-13, if the tenant fixes the problem before the date in the notice, the rental agreement does not end. If substantially the same breach comes back within six months, the landlord may terminate on at least 14 days of notice.

Unless a lease sets a fixed term, tenancy is week to week for tenants who pay weekly and month to month in every other case. A landlord who sells to a buyer wanting the house vacant often ends up using the month-to-month notice.

What the landlord files to start the case

The landlord files a sworn affidavit or complaint and a copy of the notice that was delivered. Section 89-8-33 requires the affidavit to state the facts requiring removal and identify the dwelling address and any rent or fees owed.

After filing, the court issues a summons. Section 89-8-35 requires the summons to tell the tenant that the judge will decide whether the landlord is entitled to possession, that a tenant who loses has at least seven days from the judgment to move out unless the judge sets a different period, and that a tenant sued for nonpayment can stop the eviction by paying everything owed. Service follows the Mississippi Rules of Court.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Mississippi house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

The hearing and what the judge can order

The statute puts a hard outer limit on the hearing. Section 89-8-41 lets either side ask for an adjournment, but a single adjournment cannot exceed ten days unless both parties consent, and no adjournment can push the entire hearing past 30 days from the date the case was filed.

Other points the statute sets out:

  • The court must grant a default judgment if the landlord filed the required papers, the summons was properly served, and the tenant did not appear (89-8-37).
  • Judgments must be signed and executed on the same business day they are granted.
  • If the landlord wins, the judge orders the tenant to vacate within seven days unless an emergency or other compelling circumstance justifies a shorter or longer period (89-8-39).
  • A shorter period can be justified when the tenant committed a substantial health or safety violation or poses an immediate risk of damage or injury.

Because the chapter was amended in 2022 and again in 2025, call the court clerk in the county where the house is to confirm current timing.

After the move-out date

Only law enforcement can remove a tenant, and only under a warrant. After the court-ordered move-out date the landlord may request a warrant of removal, and on payment of fees the judge issues it to the sheriff or a constable of the county.

The statute adds details that matter to owners. A warrant is not executed when it is simply posted on the door. Officers must remove the occupants and put the landlord in physical possession. For 72 hours afterward the landlord must give the tenant reasonable access to collect belongings. After that, remaining property may be moved to the curb or another agreed location.

In a case based only on unpaid rent, Section 89-8-39 bars the warrant if the tenant has paid in full all unpaid rent and other sums awarded by the move-out date, and it obliges the landlord to accept that payment in good faith. Appeals follow the Mississippi Rules of Court under 89-8-43.

How an eviction affects selling a rented house

It affects timing, cost, and what condition the house is in when you hand it over. A landlord who wants to sell has three realistic paths, and each one has a different clock.

  • Give a notice to end the tenancy, then sell once the house is vacant.
  • File for eviction because of unpaid rent or a breach, then sell after possession is returned.
  • Sell the house with the tenant in place and let the buyer deal with the lease.

Read the lease before choosing the third path. Do not shut off utilities, change locks, or remove belongings to force a move. The statute routes possession through a court judgment and a warrant.

A cash buyer can buy a rented house as-is, including one that needs repairs after a difficult tenancy. The sale does not remove any court deadline that has already started, and nobody should promise you a closing date until the possession question is clear.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Mississippi houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Property tax classes for a rental house

A rented single-family house is taxed differently from the owner's own home. Class I is single-family, owner-occupied residential real property assessed at 10 percent of true value, and Class II is all other real property at 15 percent.

Homestead exemption also requires that the applicant own and occupy the home as a primary residence on January 1. A landlord who moves out and rents the house generally cannot keep claiming it. The county Tax Assessor makes the final call, so ask that office if you are unsure.

Property tax is due by February 1 for the preceding assessment year, and an unpaid balance can lead to the county tax sale. Check for a delinquent balance before you list a rental, especially if the tenant stopped paying and the house sat in dispute for months.

Frequently asked questions

How many days notice is needed to evict for unpaid rent in Mississippi?

Three days. Under Section 89-8-13(5) the landlord delivers written notice that the rental agreement will end if rent is not paid within three days. Email or text works only if the tenant agreed in writing.

How long does a Mississippi eviction take?

The hearing cannot be adjourned beyond 30 days from the filing date under Section 89-8-41, and a tenant who loses generally gets seven days to move out. Total time also depends on notice, service, and how soon the sheriff or constable acts on the warrant.

Can a landlord change the locks to evict a tenant?

No. The statute provides a court judgment and a warrant of removal served by the sheriff or a constable. A warrant posted on the door is not executed, and officers must physically put the landlord in possession.

Can a tenant stop an eviction by paying?

In a nonpayment case, yes. Section 89-8-39 says the judge shall not issue a warrant if the tenant paid all unpaid rent and other sums awarded by the court-ordered move-out date, and the landlord must accept that payment in good faith.

Do different rules apply to commercial tenants?

Yes. Section 89-7-27 covers premises that are not a dwelling unit and allows removal after default in rent and three days of written notice, among other grounds. Residential cases use Chapter 8.

Mississippi Quitclaim Deed: Recording, Fees and When It Works

Cash Home Buyers in Mississippi
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Mississippi Quitclaim Deed sale
  • Turn the Mississippi Quitclaim Deed offer down and you owe us nothing

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Mississippi?

Where to record the deed

A quitclaim deed gets recorded with the chancery clerk of the county where the land sits. Miss. Code 89-5-1 says a conveyance of land is not good against a purchaser for valuable consideration without notice, or against any creditor, unless it is lodged with the clerk of the chancery court of that county.

The chancery clerk is custodian of the public land records, taking in, indexing and storing every record of who owns what. Tax assessors use those records to learn who owns a parcel, and tax collectors use them to learn who owes. A deed that never reaches the clerk can leave the tax bill in the old owner's name.

Clerks do not all take documents the same way. Several post separate pages on recording requirements and electronic filing, so look up your own county before making the drive.

What happens if the deed is not recorded?

A deed left unrecorded still ties the signers to it, but a person who records first can come out ahead. Under 89-5-3, conveyances of land are void against creditors and later purchasers for valuable consideration without notice unless they are acknowledged or proved and lodged with the chancery clerk.

Between the parties and their heirs, and against later purchasers who had notice or paid nothing of value, the instrument remains valid and binding. Priority follows the order of filing when nobody had actual notice.

  • Recording protects the person who received the deed.
  • Because priority runs by filing time, a delay matters if two deeds exist for one house.
  • The deed must be acknowledged or proved before it is lodged for record.

Every deed in the chain of title needs to be on record before a title company will insure. Say a parent handed the house to a child by unrecorded quitclaim years back: a buyer will want that fixed before closing.

Format rules for recording

Miss. Code 89-5-24 sets physical standards for a deed presented for recording. A deed that falls short can still be recorded, for an extra $10 per document or instrument, and a format failure does not affect validity or enforceability.

  • Pages: printed on one side only and not permanently bound.
  • Type: no smaller than ten-point.
  • Paper: white, at least twenty-pound weight.
  • Signatures: black or blue ink, with the name typed or printed beneath.
  • Top margin of page one: at least three inches left clear for the recorder.
  • All other margins: at least three-fourths of an inch.

Below that three-inch margin, the first page must show the name, business mailing address and business or employment phone number of whoever prepared the document, plus the name, mailing address and phone number of every grantor and grantee. A return address, the document title and the legal description or indexing instruction also belong there.

Documents signed before July 1, 2009, certified copies from a court or agency, and documents where an original party is deceased or incapacitated are exempt. Some clerks add that, because of the amended section, they will not accept handwritten documents.

Recording fees

Expect $25 in counties without the archive fee and $26 in counties that charge it, for up to five pages. The schedule reflects changes effective January 1, 2020 under Miss. Code 25-7-9.

Typical recording charges for a quitclaim deed
Recording chargeArchive-fee countyNon-archive county
Quitclaim deed, first five pages, with indexing$26.00$25.00
Each page beyond five$1.00$1.00
Nonconforming format surcharge (89-5-24)$10.00$10.00

Rankin, Hinds, Madison, Lowndes and Harrison are among the counties collecting the $1 archive fee. DeSoto is not. Mineral stamp fees apply in some cases, with a $1.00 minimum, and the clerk works out the actual total at recording, which can differ from an online estimate. Call the clerk before you mail a check.

Homestead exemption and the tax bill

A change of ownership can require a new homestead application. Deed changes sit on the list of triggers alongside marriage, divorce and death.

Owners must own and occupy the home on January 1 of the year they claim the exemption, and the ownership instrument has to be filed with the Chancery Clerk before January 7 for that year. Applications go to the county Tax Assessor between January 1 and April 1.

  • Because of the January 7 rule, the timing of a family deed can affect that year's exemption.
  • A disallowance can mean repaying the exemption received in error.
  • Property tax is assessed to the owner of record on January 1 and due by February 1.

Our Mississippi homestead exemption guide and property tax guide go further into these dates.

Using a quitclaim in a house sale

Think of a quitclaim as a hand-off of whatever the signer happens to own, nothing more. It does not establish that the signer can sell the whole house. Whether it helps in a sale turns on who is currently on title and whether any court step remains open.

  • Among family members who already own the house, it can add or remove a name, if the deed is properly acknowledged and recorded.
  • For an inherited house, the heirs usually deal with the estate first. See our Mississippi probate guide.
  • If a spouse or co-owner is involved, ask a Mississippi attorney about marital and homestead rights before anyone signs.
  • If a loan or tax lien is attached, ask the title company how it will be paid off before closing.

Warranties and title insurance are a separate matter, and a quitclaim typically carries no promise about title. Talk to a Mississippi real estate attorney or title company before relying on one in a sale.

A title company usually starts by searching the clerk's records back through earlier owners. Any gap, such as a deed that was signed but never filed, tends to surface at that point and can push back a closing date. Sorting out the deed history before listing gives you room to fix a gap without a buyer waiting on you.

We buy Mississippi houses as-is and reply with a written offer. If the deed is the open question, we can talk through what the chancery clerk's records show before anyone signs.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Mississippi houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Steps to record a quitclaim deed

  1. Fill in the deed with the preparer's information, all parties, a return address and the legal description.
  2. Sign in black or blue ink in front of someone who can take the acknowledgment.
  3. Check the page count and format so no surcharge is added.
  4. Call the chancery clerk in the county where the land lies to confirm the total fee and whether e-recording is available.
  5. File it quickly, because the earlier filing wins a priority contest.

Frequently asked questions

Is a quitclaim deed valid in Mississippi if it is not recorded?

Yes, as to the signers and their heirs. But under section 89-5-3 a later buyer who paid value without notice, or a creditor, can beat it if it was never lodged with the chancery clerk.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Mississippi?

For a quitclaim deed the published fee is $25 in non-archive counties and $26 in archive-fee counties for the first five pages, plus $1 for each extra page. The clerk calculates the final amount at recording.

What must be on the first page of a Mississippi deed?

Below the three-inch top margin: who prepared it (name, business address, phone), every grantor and grantee with address and phone, a return address, the document title and the legal description.

Do I need a notary for a quitclaim deed in Mississippi?

Section 89-5-3 requires a conveyance to be acknowledged or proved before it is lodged with the clerk if it is to be good against creditors and later purchasers. Ask the clerk's office who can take the acknowledgment.

Will a quitclaim deed change my homestead exemption?

It can. Deed changes may require a new homestead application, and the ownership instrument must be filed with the Chancery Clerk before January 7 of the year the exemption is claimed.

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Mississippi Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property sale

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Mississippi?

Which court handles probate

Probate here goes through the chancery court, and which county's court depends on where the person lived. Under Miss. Code 91-7-1, a will is proved and letters testamentary are issued by the chancery court of the county where the testator had a fixed place of residence.

When there was no fixed residence and the will leaves land, the right court is the chancery court of the county where the land, or part of it, lies. If someone died without a will, Miss. Code 91-7-63 points to the county where the person lived at death. With no fixed residence, it points to the county where the person died or where some of the personal property sits.

The chapter reaches the property of people who were domiciled in Mississippi and the Mississippi real estate of nonresidents (Section 91-1-1). An heir in another state who inherits a house here still goes through a Mississippi chancery court for that house.

Probate routes for an estate that owns a house

Heirs of a homeowner generally meet one of four routes. Letters testamentary and letters of administration open full administration. A will admitted as a muniment of title clears land without an executor. A successor affidavit handles small personal property only. Only the first three can touch real estate.

Mississippi probate routes
RouteWhat it doesLimit or trigger
Letters testamentary (91-7-1)Court admits the will and appoints an executorChancery court of the county of residence
Letters of administration (91-7-63)Court appoints an administrator when there is no willRelative preferred, then others; creditor or other suitable person after 30 days
Muniment of title only (91-5-35)Will admitted to clear title to devised real property, no executor or administratorProbate estate within the 91-7-322 limit, known debts paid
Successor affidavit (91-7-322)Successor collects debts or tangible personal propertyEntire probate estate no more than $75,000, at least 30 days after death

The affidavit route covers money owed to the decedent and tangible items such as a bank balance or a vehicle. Section 91-7-322 says nothing about conveying real property, so a house generally needs one of the court routes.

How a muniment of title works

A muniment of title petition lets a will that leaves Mississippi land be admitted without naming an executor or administrator. The 2020 amendment in Senate Bill 2850 rewrote section 91-5-35 and took effect July 1, 2020.

A personal representative signs and swears to the petition. If none is serving, the decedent's living spouse and the devisees of the Mississippi real property, whether specific or residuary, sign and swear to it instead. People holding only contingent remainder interests are left out.

The petition has to show two things:

  • The decedent's Mississippi probate estate, leaving out real property and exempt property, stayed within the amount in section 91-7-322, which SB 2850 raised to $75,000.
  • Every known debt of the decedent and the estate is paid, including estate and income taxes if any.

A muniment of title does not shut anyone out. An interested party can still ask for formal administration or contest the will.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Mississippi house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Who is appointed when there is no will

If someone dies intestate, the chancery court grants letters of administration to a relative who applies, with the husband or wife first in line. After that, 91-7-63 has the court turn to others next entitled to share in the estate, picking the best-suited person among equals.

The court may also choose a stranger, or a trust company or national bank doing business here, if the kindred are incompetent. If no relative applies within 30 days of death, administration can go to a creditor or another suitable person. A family hoping to sell the house should watch that 30-day mark, because a creditor could end up steering the process if relatives wait.

Creditor claims and an inherited house

Claims run on a short clock, and an unresolved one can hold up the estate even when the house has plenty of equity. Under 91-7-145, the executor or administrator must make reasonably diligent efforts to identify creditors and mail each a notice.

The representative then files an affidavit with the clerk and publishes a notice in a county newspaper for three consecutive weeks. The notice warns that any claim not probated and registered within 90 days after first publication is barred, and section 91-7-151 backs up that ninety-day cutoff.

A county without a newspaper can use posting at the courthouse door and three other places of public resort. Proof of publication goes on file before the decree of final discharge.

For heirs, the timeline looks like this:

  • Letters from the chancery court start the notice process.
  • Three weeks of publication, then 90 days from the first publication for claims.
  • Known debts, taxes, and any mortgage on the house still get dealt with before anyone sees net proceeds.

Problems heirs run into when selling

The usual trouble spots are unclear title, carrying costs while the court works, and repairs nobody wants to fund. Property tax keeps running through all of it. Taxes are assessed to the owner of record on January 1, billed in November or December, and due by the following February 1. A death in the middle of the year does not pause that cycle. Our Mississippi property tax guide covers the bill, appeals and tax sale timing.

Recording matters as well. Under 89-5-3, a conveyance is void against creditors and later purchasers for value without notice unless it is acknowledged or proved and lodged with the chancery clerk of the proper county. Between the parties and their heirs the instrument stays valid either way. Heirs who sign deeds among themselves should still record them.

  • Confirm which chancery court has the estate and who holds letters.
  • Ask the chancery clerk where the will and any petitions are filed.
  • Collect the death certificate, the will, the deed into the decedent and a recent tax bill.
  • Check for a mortgage, tax arrears or liens on the house.
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Mississippi houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Where a cash sale fits

A cash buyer does not replace probate. What changes is how the house gets sold once it is clear who has authority to sign. A personal representative holding letters, or heirs who hold title after a muniment of title, can sign a deed, and the buyer can take the house as it stands.

That can suit a vacant house, one with deferred repairs, or one in a county far from the heirs. We buy houses in Mississippi as-is and respond with a written offer. We do not promise a price in this guide, and we suggest talking to a Mississippi probate attorney about which route fits your estate.

Documents to gather first

Before calling anyone, pull together the original will if there is one, a certified death certificate, the last recorded deed, the most recent property tax bill, and any mortgage statement. The chancery clerk can tell you whether a file has already been opened. Having these in hand shortens the first meeting with an attorney and lets a buyer or title company see exactly what the estate owns.

Frequently asked questions

Do I have to probate a will in Mississippi if the house is in the will?

Usually yes. A will that leaves Mississippi real property is proved in chancery court, either with letters testamentary or, for smaller estates, as a muniment of title under section 91-5-35. The right route depends on the size of the probate estate and whether debts are paid.

What is the small estate limit for a successor affidavit in Mississippi?

The limit is $75,000 for the entire probate estate. Section 91-7-322 was amended by SB 2850, effective July 1, 2020, and the affidavit can be used at least 30 days after death. It covers debts owed to the decedent and tangible personal property, not real estate.

How long do creditors have to file claims against a Mississippi estate?

Creditors have 90 days after the first publication of the notice to present a claim. The notice runs three consecutive weeks, and known creditors must also be mailed notice.

Which county's chancery court handles my parent's estate?

Generally the county where your parent had a fixed place of residence at death. With no fixed residence and a will that leaves land, it is the county where the land lies.

Can a nonresident heir sell inherited Mississippi property?

Yes, but the real property is still handled under Mississippi law in a Mississippi court. An out-of-state heir should work with the chancery clerk's office or a Mississippi attorney to confirm who signs the deed.
